author: Tertullian
addressee: Catholic Christians who oppose the New Prophecy's fasting practices
occasion: Tertullian defends the fasting practices of the New Prophecy movement against 'psychic' critics; the opponents reject the New Prophecy specifically because it teaches frequent fasting rather than remarriage, not because they call fasting itself an innovation per se.
argument: Tertullian argues that fasting is not a novelty but a discipline grounded in God's original command to Adam, in Israel's history, and in Christ's own example. He contends that the 'psychics' who oppose stricter fasting are driven by love of food and the belly, and that their objections from Scripture are misread. He defends three practices: ieiunationes (fasts), xerophagiae (dry-food diets), and stationes (stations), with the extension of stations until evening defended as part of the station practice. He concludes that such discipline prepares Christians for martyrdom and that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, has authority to institute these observances.

outline.move: Tertullian opens by attacking his opponents as belly-driven 'psychics' who hate fasting and accuse the New Prophecy of innovation.
He summarizes the opponents' biblical arguments: only the Day of Atonement and the days when the bridegroom is absent are legitimate fasts; everything else is optional.
He grounds fasting in Adam's fall through food, arguing that abstinence from food is the remedy for the original sin of eating.
He explains why God did not impose fasting laws at first, but gradually introduced dietary restrictions after the Flood.
He shows that Israel in the wilderness rejected the manna (dry angelic bread) and longed for Egyptian foods; God punished their gluttony and used this to train them in continence.
He argues from nature and Scripture that a full belly dulls the mind; he cites Moses as one who fasted and saw God's glory, and Elijah as another fasting companion of the Lord.
He gives examples of fasting's power: Samuel's victory, Hezekiah's deliverance, Nineveh's repentance, Ahab's reprieve, Hannah's son, and Daniel's revelations.

He turns to the New Testament: Anna the prophetess, Christ's dedication of his baptism by fasting, teaching that some demons are cast out by fasting, Cornelius's fasting being heard, and Paul enumerating many fasts among his labors.

He defends xerophagies from Daniel and his brothers preferring vegetables and water; Elijah receiving bread and water; David's penitential diet; Samuel's and Aaron's abstinence from wine; and Timothy's wine abstinence out of devotion.
He defends stations extended until evening, arguing from Peter's example, the Lord's passion, and Old Testament precedents like Moses, Joshua, Saul, and Daniel.
He argues that whether these practices come from the Spirit or from human devotion, they are legitimate because they serve the same God as the old observances.
He contrasts his opponents' luxurious lifestyle with the discipline needed for martyrdom, mocking their pampered 'martyr' Pristinus.

He argues that his opponents themselves practice voluntary fasts and stations outside tradition, doing so by choice not command; and that the Holy Spirit as Paraclete/Advocate commanded such observances providentially for impending trials.
He answers the charge of 'Galatianism' by distinguishing Christian observances from Jewish legal ceremonies.
He answers that Paul approved those who abstain in honor of God, not those who do so in contempt of the Creator; and that while all foods are permitted, the kingdom of God is not food and drink.
He gives further examples of punishment for gluttony and of fasting's honor, including the rich man and Lazarus, Joel's call, and pagan parallels.
He concludes with a satirical portrait of his opponents as Esau-like gluttons, and exhorts Christians to embrace fasting as preparation for death and resurrection.

cast.name: Tertullian
cast.who: The author, a Christian writer defending the fasting practices of the New Prophecy.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first man, whose sin of eating brought death and made fasting the remedy.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: The lawgiver who fasted forty days and received the law.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: The prophet who fasted forty days and met God at Horeb.

cast.name: Daniel
cast.who: The prophet whose fasts and dry-food diet brought him revelations.

cast.name: Samuel
cast.who: The prophet whose fasting people won victory over the Philistines.

cast.name: Hezekiah
cast.who: The king whose humiliation and fasting saved Jerusalem from Sennacherib.

cast.name: Ahab
cast.who: The king whose fasting after Naboth's murder postponed God's judgment.

cast.name: Hannah
cast.who: The wife of Elkanah whose fasting obtained a son, Samuel.

cast.name: Anna the prophetess
cast.who: Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, who recognized the infant Lord and spoke about him to those awaiting Israel's redemption, and whose fasting was added to her title of long-standing and once-married widowhood.

cast.name: Cornelius
cast.who: The centurion whose fasting was heard by God before his baptism.

cast.name: Timothy
cast.who: Paul's disciple who abstained from wine out of devotion.

cast.name: Pristinus
cast.who: A non-Christian martyr whom Tertullian's opponents pampered in prison with baths and luxuries, then drugged with wine on trial day so that he couldn't answer the governor's question about confessing the Lord, and died in denial with only hiccups and belches.

cast.name: Montanus
cast.who: A prophet of the New Prophecy whose teachings included frequent fasting.

cast.name: Priscilla
cast.who: A prophetess of the New Prophecy.

cast.name: Maximilla
cast.who: A prophetess of the New Prophecy.

cast.name: Marcion
cast.who: A heretic who commanded perpetual abstinence from foods, despising the Creator's works.

cast.name: Tatian
cast.who: A heretic associated with extreme abstinence.

cast.name: Apicius
cast.who: A famous gourmet/glutton, used satirically: 'Why do you hesitate to believe in the Paraclete whom you deny in Montanus, but believe in Apicius?' — the point is that they already follow a 'paraclete' of gluttony.

voices.speaker: Opponents (psychics)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases like 'obiectant' (they object), 'opponunt' (they set against), 'dicunt' (they say), 'dicis' (you say), 'obducitur' (is brought forward), 'reprobat' (he reproves = they object), 'incusant' (they accuse)

voices.speaker: Scripture (Old and New Testament)
voices.how_marked: Quoted directly with introductory formulas like 'he says', 'it is written', 'the Lord says'

voices.speaker: The Paraclete (Holy Spirit)
voices.how_marked: Referred to as the one against whom the psychics make controversy, who commands the New Prophecy's observances, and as Advocate (paracletus = aduocatus) who intercedes for the church

key_terms.sense: Tertullian's derogatory term for mainstream Christians who live by the soul rather than the Spirit, opposing the New Prophecy's discipline
Dry-food diets: abstaining from meat, juicy foods, and wine, eating only dry bread and water
Weekly fast days on Wednesday and Friday, which Tertullian's group extended until evening
The Holy Spirit as advocate and revealer, whom Tertullian claims authorizes the New Prophecy's observances
Gluttony or the belly's appetite, the root sin behind opposition to fasting
Self-control, especially in food and marriage, the discipline Tertullian defends
Fasting, the central practice under discussion, both commanded and voluntary
The New Prophecy movement (Montanism), which Tertullian defends
Rich feeding or fattening, the opposite of fasting, associated with spiritual dullness
Confession of sin accompanied by fasting, sackcloth, and ashes
Self-humbling before God through fasting and mourning
Leanness or thinness of body from fasting, which Tertullian praises

names.Iouem: A heretic, 'modern from Pythagoras' — possibly a follower of Pythagorean/Encratite asceticism; identity uncertain
names.Pythagora: The phrase is 'hodiernum de Pythagora haereticum' — a modern heretic derived from Pythagoras, not Pythagoras himself
names.Saulis: Of Saul (genitive), referring to King Saul, father of Jonathan
names.Corinthiorum: Second [letter] of the Corinthians — the book title
names.Galatis: With the Galatians — the people/letter, in context 'cum Galatis' means 'as with the Galatians' or 'along with [the letter to] the Galatians'
names.Actis: In the Acts — the book of Acts

scripture: Tertullian uses the Septuagint (LXX) book names and Psalm numbering, citing books as Leuiticus, Esaias, Hieremias, Iohel, and legum Naue (Joshua). Modern citations should use standard English Bible names (Leviticus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Joel, Joshua) and LXX Psalm numbering where applicable.
uncertain: The exact date of composition; it is placed in Tertullian's Montanist period, c. 208–212 AD, but cannot be fixed precisely.
Whether the 'Pristinus' incident refers to a specific historical martyr or is a rhetorical invention.
The precise identity of 'Iouem' as a heretic; it may refer to a follower of Tatian or another Encratite teacher.
Whether Tertullian's opponents were a specific group or a general characterization of mainstream Carthaginian Christians.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the opponents reject the New Prophecy specifically because it teaches frequent fasting rather than remarriage, not because they call fasting itself an innovation per se
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: non quod alium deum praedicent Montanus et Priscilla et Maximilla, nec quod Iesum Christum soluant, nec quod aliquam fidei aut spei regulam euertant, sed quod plane doceant saepius ieiunare quam nubere
_unresolved_facts.fix: The opponents reject the New Prophecy because it teaches frequent fasting rather than remarriage (saepius ieiunare quam nubere), but they DO call fasting itself an innovation: 'nouitatem igitur obiectant' (they object novelty), 'de cuius inlicito praescribant' (concerning its unlawfulness they prescribe), and demand it be judged heresy or pseudoprophecy. The brief should say they reject it both because of the specific emphasis on fasting over remarriage AND because they treat these fasting practices as unlawful novelties.

_unresolved_facts.claim: with the extension of stations until evening defended as part of the station practice
_unresolved_facts.fix: Tertullian defends extending stations 'plerumque in uesperam' (mostly/often until evening), not as a universal rule but as a frequent practice. The brief should note this is one of three practices (ieiunationes, xerophagiae, stationes) and that the evening extension is specifically defended as 'serae stationis' (late stations) with multiple possible rationales, not simply 'part of the station practice.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections 9: He defends xerophagies from Daniel and his brothers preferring vegetables and water; Elijah receiving bread and water; David's penitential diet; Samuel's and Aaron's abstinence from wine; and Timothy's wine abstinence out of devotion.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief misrepresents Timothy. Tertullian says Timothy abstained from wine 'non ex institutione, sed ex deuotione' (not from institution/rule, but from devotion), but Paul advised him 'modico uino uti' (to use a little wine) for his stomach and frequent illnesses. Tertullian uses this to argue that Paul's advice against abstinence for necessity's sake actually commends abstinence as devotion to God. The brief should clarify: Timothy's abstinence was from devotion, not Paul's command; Paul actually advised wine for health reasons.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections 13: He argues that his opponents themselves practice voluntary fasts and stations outside tradition, doing so by choice not command
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ecce enim conuenio uos et praeter pascha ieiunantes citra illos dies, quibus ablatus est sponsus, et stationum semiieiunia interponentes, et uos interdum pane et aqua uictitantes, ut cuique uisum est. denique respondetis haec ex arbitrio agenda, non ex imperio
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief should specify that Tertullian says opponents fast 'praeter pascha' (besides Passover), observe 'stationum semiieiunia' (half-fast stations), and sometimes live on bread and water 'ut cuique uisum est' (as it seemed good to each one). They claim these are 'ex arbitrio agenda, non ex imperio' (to be done by choice, not by command). The brief's 'outside tradition' is not quite right—Tertullian says they exceed tradition ('excedendo traditionem').

_unresolved_facts.claim: Pristinus: 'A non-Christian martyr whom Tertullian's opponents pampered in prison with baths and luxuries, then drugged with wine on trial day so that he couldn't answer the governor's question about confessing the Lord, and died in denial with only hiccups and belches.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: quem ex facultate custodiae liberae aliquamdiu fartum, omnibus balneis quasi baptismate melioribus et omnibus luxuriae secessibus quasi ecclesia secretioribus et omnibus uitae istius inlecebris quasi aeterna dignioribus hoc puto obligatum mori uellet, postremo ipso tribunalis die luce summa condito mero tamquam antidoto praemedicatum ita eneruastis, ut paucis ungulis titillatus (hoc enim ebrietas sentiebat) quem dominum confiteretur interroganti praesidi respondere non potuerit amplius, atque ita de hoc iam extortus, cum singultus et ructus solos haberet, in ipsa negatione discessit
_unresolved_facts.fix: Pristinus was 'non Christianus martyr' (not a Christian martyr)—correct. But Tertullian says opponents 'fartum' (stuffed him) with luxuries, thinking this would 'obligatum mori uellet' (make him obligated to die/want to die). They 'eneruastis' (enervated/weakened him) with wine 'tamquam antidoto praemedicatum' (as if pre-medicated with antidote). The key error: he didn't 'die in denial with only hiccups and belches'—he 'in ipsa negatione discessit' (departed in the very act of denial), with 'singultus et ructus solos haberet' (having only hiccups and belches [instead of words]). He couldn't answer the governor's question about whom he confessed as Lord, and thus was 'extortus' (wrenched/extracted) from this [situation/life] in denial. The brief should say he was unable to confess and died in denial, not that he 'couldn't answer' in the sense of being incapacitated then dying of that—the wine caused his inability to speak, leading to his denial.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: piget iam cum talibus congredi, pudet etiam de eis altercari
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 12 does NOT contain opponent voices. It is entirely Tertullian's own invective against his opponents' lifestyle and their treatment of Pristinus, with no 'dicunt,' 'dicis,' or similar markers. The brief should remove 12 from the opponents' voice sections. Also, section 16 contains some opponent-like objections ('tu nostris xerophagiis blasphemias ingerens'), but these are embedded in Tertullian's rhetoric rather than formal opponent quotations.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ut ab Iohanne paracletus obmutuisset, et ipsi nobis prophetae in hanc maxime causam extitissemus
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 12 does NOT contain the Paraclete as a speaking voice. Tertullian hypothetically says 'ut ab Iohanne paracletus obmutuisset' (as if the Paraclete had fallen silent from John [onward]), but this is counterfactual—he is saying even if the Paraclete were silent, Christians would still need to practice discipline. The Paraclete is mentioned but not as a present voice. Section 12 should be removed from the Paraclete's voice sections.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Iouem: 'A heretic, 'modern from Pythagoras' — possibly a follower of Pythagorean/Encratite asceticism; identity uncertain'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: apud Iouem, hodiernum de Pythagora haereticum
_unresolved_facts.fix: The name is 'Iouem' (Jove/Jupiter) used as a person's name, not the god. The phrase is 'hodiernum de Pythagora haereticum' (a modern heretic from Pythagoras). The brief correctly notes this is not Pythagoras himself, but 'Iouem' is a personal name (possibly a Latinized form or nickname), not 'Jove' the god. The uncertainty note is appropriate but the name form should be clarified: this is a named individual, not the deity.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Galatis: 'With the Galatians — the people/letter, in context 'cum Galatis' means 'as with the Galatians' or 'along with [the letter to] the Galatians''
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: sic et cum Galatis nos quoque percuti aiunt obseruatores dierum et mensium et annorum
_unresolved_facts.fix: In context, 'cum Galatis' means 'as with the Galatians' or 'along with the Galatians'—the opponents strike Tertullian's side 'as also with the Galatians,' accusing them of being 'obseruatores dierum et mensium et annorum' (observers of days and months and years). The brief's note is actually correct in substance, but the formulation 'cum Galatis nos quoque percuti aiunt' means 'they say we too are struck/beaten along with the Galatians,' i.e., the same charge applied to Galatians is applied to Tertullian's group. The brief's rendering is acceptable but slightly awkward.
